analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional districts with independent commissions and hold open primaries.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced January 2023, it was referred to two House committees and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The CLEAN Elections Act would require every state to draw its congressional maps using an independent, nonpartisan commission — with equal numbers of members from the two largest parties and no elected officials on it — and to hold open primaries, meaning any registered voter could vote in any party's primary. To push states on their own legislative maps and primaries, the bill would make federal election-administration money conditional on states adopting the same rules for state and local elections.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, especially in states where one party currently draws its own district lines or where independent voters are barred from voting in party primaries. Nonpartisan commissions tend to produce more competitive districts, which gives voters real choices, and open primaries let the roughly independent and unaffiliated voters help pick the candidates who appear on the November ballot.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in gerrymandered states and independents

how_it_helps.text: Requires congressional redistricting to be done by a nonpartisan independent commission with equal members from the two largest parties and no elected officials, taking map-drawing away from the legislators whose seats the maps affect.
Requires open primaries for federal elections, so any registered voter can cast a ballot in any party's primary rather than being locked out by party registration rules.

Conditions federal election-administration funds on states certifying that they also use independent commissions for state legislative districts and hold open primaries for state and local office, extending the same rules beyond Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress, state legislators, and the two major party organizations, which today control how district lines are drawn and who can vote in the primaries that effectively decide most House and state legislative seats.

drawbacks.text: The federal mandate reaches into how states run their own elections for state and local office, by making federal election funding conditional — a significant use of federal spending power over state election systems that states may resist on federalism grounds.

The open-primary requirement would force political parties to let non-members vote in their nomination contests, including for convention delegates and presidential preference primaries, which party organizations argue puts nomination choices in the hands of voters who are not affiliated with the party.

The bill requires commissions to be partisan-balanced and free of elected officials, but it does not specify how commission members are selected or how a commission's plan is adopted, leaving open questions about how independent such commissions would be in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — taking map-drawing away from the officials whose seats depend on the maps — directly serves voters and would cost incumbents their grip on seat selection, which is exactly why it draws resistance. The open-primary mandate is more contested: it expands participation but forces parties to accept outside voters in their nominations. The funding condition on state and local elections is the most legally aggressive part and the weakest link. On balance, the bill aims at a real driver of uncompetitive elections, though its enforcement by funding conditions is blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Administration and Judiciary committees in January 2023, and neither committee took it up — no markup, no vote, nothing — before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican, introduced the CLEAN Elections Act on January 9, 2023, requiring independent nonpartisan redistricting commissions and open primaries for federal elections.
The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee and additionally to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no other cosponsors joined.
No further action of any kind — no committee consideration, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and the two major parties, who keep control of drawing congressional maps and of primary electorates, the two levers that decide most House seats without general-election competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents and party leaders who kept map control

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred, so no party split was recorded; the only recorded support was a Republican sponsor plus a single Democratic cosponsor, and the bill died quietly in committee rather than through an open party fight.

industries.note: The bill would take congressional map-drawing away from the legislators whose seats the maps determine and give it to nonpartisan commissions, weakening the incumbency protection built into gerrymandered districts. Its failure preserves that protection.

Parties currently set primary rules that exclude non-members, in many districts the only election that matters, and party-controlled map drawing. Open primaries and independent commissions would take both levers away.
